0.0.n: さん adds politeness when addressing the audience as a group.

0.2.n: A standard daytime greeting; the final は is pronounced わ.

1.0.n: This country name is followed by に to show where Sakura lives.

1.1.n: に marks the place where someone lives when used with 住む.

1.2.n: The plain form of 住む comes before サクラ to describe her as someone who lives in Japan.

1.3.n: This is the speaker’s name, written in katakana.

1.4.n: です ends the self-introduction politely; the speaker leaves out I.

2.0.n: The speaker uses her own name here rather than saying me.

2.1.n: と marks the person joining you in an activity.

2.2.n: 一緒 combines with に to describe doing an activity jointly.

2.3.n: に completes 一緒に, making it describe how the activity is done.

2.5.n: 日本語 names the language being practiced.

2.6.n: の links 日本語 to the listening and speaking skills that follow.

2.7.n: This English loanword refers to understanding spoken language as a skill.

2.8.n: と joins the two skills, リスニング and スピーキング.

2.9.n: This English loanword refers to producing spoken language as a skill.

2.10.n: を marks both listening and speaking as what the proposed action will improve.

2.11.n: 上達する means to get better; させる means make something improve, and ましょう politely proposes doing it together.

0.tip: 皆さん politely addresses a whole audience.

1.lit: Am Sakura who lives in Japan.
1.tip: 日本に住む comes before the name it describes, unlike English who lives in Japan.

2.lit: Together with Sakura, let’s improve Japanese listening and speaking.
2.tip: ましょう makes this a polite invitation to improve together, rather than a command.
